newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: WTO ministers make major push to seal infotech deal.
newsitem.headline: WTO ministers make major push to seal infotech deal.

text.p: World Trade Organisation (WTO) ministers were making a major push on Monday to wrap up a deal by Friday that would eliminate tariffs on a wide range of information technology.

Singapore Trade Minister Yeo Cheow Tong, chairman of the first meeting of WTO ministers, urged them to "apply themselves to the task of concluding an agreement on information technology products by the end of this meeting," a WTO spokesman said.

Acting U.S Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, who hopes to make the Information Technology Agreement (ITA) the crowning achievement of this week's WTO ministerial meeting, and European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan met to try to thrash out their differences over the types of products that would be covered by the agreement.
Deputy U.S. Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang told reporters the discussions "provided a basis for moving forward." But he added that there was "still a lot of difficult work to do."
Barshefsky and Brittan were to continue their talks on Monday night and again over breakfast Tuesday morning.

Barshefsky told the WTO meeting an ITA, which would eliminate duties on hundreds of products including computers and telecommunications equipment, would help businesses become more competitive in the global economy by putting lower-cost equipment and information into their hands.

"That's why we must reach an agreement this week," she said in a speech to the opening session. "Remaining issues are ripe for discussion. We have an historic opportunity to eliminate tariffs on these products. We must seize it."
Brittan said an ITA pact was vital to the success of the WTO gathering, along with progress towards a WTO pact opening up telecommunications markets.

"I should not have to say that we all have to make a further effort. But we do. If we do not make substantial progress on both issues this week, with new offers tabled, then our meeting will not be the big success we all want," he told the WTO meeting.
While efforts to strike a deal by the end of the WTO ministerial on Friday shifted into high gear, it remained uncertain whether the ministers would be successful in their efforts.

"We've just gotten started so it's too early to say what the outlook is, but we somehow want to reach an agreement during the ministerial meeting," a Japanese trade official told reporters. "From early morning to late in the evening, we are making efforts...I think that a lot of momentum has emerged."
Japan on Monday joined the United States in suggesting that Brussels was an obstacle to an infotechnology agreement.

"The main obstacle is the European Union," a Japanese official said. He said Tokyo was concerned over an EU effort to link the elimination of tariffs to non-tariff issues, such as further liberalisation of government procurement.

The United States has accused the European Union of dragging its feet on the ITA, but EU officials have pointed to the Americans' desire to exclude four products -- capacitors, graphic tubes, photocopiers and fibre optics -- as a major obstacle.
These four products represented only $13 billion of the $595 billion worth of IT products exported last year.

Developing countries want more flexibility on the timetable for eliminating tariffs on infotech products and Singapore's Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong told reporters: "I think there will be an agreement but not an agreement on zero tariffs by 2000."
Australian deputy premier and trade minister Tim Fischer said there were still a lot of negotiations proceeding at the margins.
"I think there are a few balls up in the air at 12-noon on day one and we will have to wait and see," said Fischer.

For Japan, a key issue was also the number of countries, particularly Asian-Pacific nations -- that would join the ITA pact. Not all WTO members are expected to join the agreement, but ITA supporters hope that a sufficient number would join to make it worthwhile.

One U.S. businessman lobbying for the ITA said he would be "very disappointed" if no deal was forged. "I am bullish but not cocky," said Aaron Cross, public policy director at International Business Machines (IBM).
